_readme: STANDING EXAMPLES: platform-authored worked examples, seeded per module so a
founder who turns a module on sees what it is FOR instead of 'No items yet.'
Every row seeded from this file carries is_example = 1 and is INERT: it renders
in full, and every mutation against it is refused. Nothing here ever reaches the
ledger, escrow, Stripe, or the capability gate.
Copy is deliberately platform-generic, no village's brand, so every fork
inherits the same examples and scripts/check-brand-refs.mjs stays green.
Retirement: the first real item published in a module deletes that module's

_note: Examples need authors. These are is_example = 1 rows in `users` with no
password_hash, so they can never log in, and they are excluded from member
lists, launch member counts, gratitude eligibility, the Sybil helper, badge
evaluation and health snapshots. The '(example)' suffix is load-bearing: the
tombstone precedent in anonymizeMember() is that a real row whose display
name carries the meaning beats a special type.

circles.name: Land & Water
circles.purpose: Holds everything the ground itself asks for: soil, water catchment, planting cycles, and the long repair of what was farmed hard before us. Decisions about what gets planted where start here.

circles.name: Welcome & Belonging
circles.purpose: The first face a visitor meets and the people who notice when someone has gone quiet. Runs arrivals, orientation, conflict repair, and the rhythms that keep a group of strangers becoming a community.

circles.name: Build & Repair
circles.purpose: Structures, tools, power and water infrastructure. Everything that has to physically work by Tuesday. Also the circle that decides when something should be repaired and when it should be replaced.

map._memberTrigger: The first circle a founder creates clears them.

progression._note: Roles have no POST route; these seed alongside roles-seed.json only into an empty table.

roles.name: Land Steward
roles.description: Walks the land weekly, keeps the planting calendar honest, and is the person a quest about soil or water should be routed to. Holds no budget authority, which stays with the circle.

roles.name: Welcome Host
roles.description: Meets arrivals, runs the first-week orientation, and checks in at day thirty. The role most villages under-staff and most regret under-staffing.

roles.name: Tool Keeper
roles.description: Knows where every shared tool is, what condition it is in, and who had it last. If the Material Library module is on, this is the role that signs items in and out.

progression._memberTrigger: The first role this village writes for itself clears them.
progression._orgRolesNote: Seats for the village map (0049). The roles array above is the PERMISSION-GROUP table and is a different thing entirely; these are the sociocratic seats the map draws. Holders are documented names, never accounts, so an example seat can never point at a real person.

orgRoles.name: Land Steward
orgRoles.aim: Keep the land legible: what grows where, what needs water, and what the season is asking for next.
orgRoles.domain: Planting plans, water, soil, and the rhythm of the growing year.
accountabilities: Walks the land weekly and writes down what changed
Calls the work parties the season needs
Holds the planting plan and keeps it honest
orgRoles.whyItMatters: Land nobody is watching drifts, and by the time it shows it has usually been drifting a while.

orgRoles.name: Welcome Host
orgRoles.aim: Be the first warm face, so nobody arrives and has to work out who to ask.
orgRoles.domain: Arrivals, orientation, and the first month of somebody being here.
accountabilities: Meets each new arrival within their first week
Hands newcomers on to the circle that fits them
orgRoles.whyItMatters: How somebody is met in their first month decides whether there is a second year.

orgRoles.name: Tool Keeper
orgRoles.aim: Every tool findable, sharp, and back where the next person will look for it.
orgRoles.domain: The tool store, repairs, and what the village still needs to buy or borrow.
accountabilities: Checks the store after each work party
Repairs or retires what is broken
Says plainly when a job needs a tool the village does not have
orgRoles.whyItMatters: A blunt saw nobody mentions costs more hours than the saw did.

quests._trigger: POST /api/admin/quests creates a real quest and retires the rest, and so does accepting a quest proposal. POST /api/admin/quests/:id/keep turns ONE starter real and leaves the others standing.
quests._note: The starter board every fresh village opens on (Rye, sheet A8 / 19g: a neutral, fully editable starter set). The ONE source of truth for a new village's quests: server/seeds/quests-seed.json is frozen and seeds nothing. Seeds only where the village has no quest and no claim of its own. No reward label and no value: a quest's value is set on its card by the village, when a founder keeps it. Generic on purpose: no place, facility, person or price that one village has and another may not.

quests.title: Welcome someone new
quests.subtitle: Be the first hello a newcomer remembers.
quests.description: Meet a newcomer at their first gathering or visit. Show them around, answer what you can, and introduce them to a few people by name.
quests.impact: People stay where somebody learned their name in the first week.
quests.story: Most people decide how they feel about a place within their first hour. Whoever welcomes them shapes that hour: a nervous arrival becomes someone who knows three names, where to find water, and what happens next.
quests.firstStep: At the next gathering, introduce yourself to one person you have never met.
steps: Pick an upcoming gathering and plan to arrive early.
Greet newcomers as they arrive, learn their names, and show them the essentials.
Answer their questions honestly, and note the ones you could not answer.
Before you leave, introduce each newcomer to someone who shares one of their interests.
Check in with them a week later.
quests.deliverable: A few lines on who you welcomed and one thing that would make the next arrival smoother.
tips: Name tags feel small until you watch someone relax because they can read the room.
Most questions from a newcomer are really asking where they fit. Answer that one.
quests.duration: One gathering, and a check-in a week later

quests.title: Host a shared meal
quests.subtitle: Set the table and let the village happen.
quests.description: Plan and host a potluck or shared meal. Pick a date and a place, invite widely, sort out who brings what, and gather a crew to set up and clean up.
quests.impact: Friendships start and plans take shape over shared food.
quests.story: Shared meals are where a village becomes real. People who only nod at each other in meetings end up talking for an hour over the second helping. Hosting one well is logistics in service of a good evening.
quests.firstStep: Pick a date that is clear on the calendar and write one sentence about the gathering.
steps: Choose the date, the place and a theme if you want one.
Invite widely: the board, the feed and a few personal asks each reach different people.
Coordinate who brings what, plus a crew to set up and a crew to clean up.
Host the evening: welcome people, open the meal, and keep an eye on anyone new.
Thank the helpers and note what to repeat or drop next time.
quests.deliverable: A short recap: who came, what was shared, and what you would repeat.
tips: Plan the cleanup crew before the meal, never during it.
A visible welcome table saves every late arrival.

quests.title: Take the notes at a circle meeting
quests.subtitle: Keep the village's memory.
quests.description: Record one circle meeting: the proposals, the decisions, who carries each action, and the questions left open. Publish the notes the same day.
quests.impact: Decisions that are written down get carried out, and newcomers can see how the village decides.
quests.story: Decisions fade and notes last. Good notes turn an evening of discussion into a record everyone can trust: what was decided, who carries it, and why.
quests.firstStep: Read the last set of published notes and list what a newcomer would still not understand.
steps: Join the meeting and capture proposals, decisions and owners as they land.
Write the notes the same day, while the detail is fresh.
Publish them where the circle keeps its records.
Flag the open questions so the next meeting starts where this one ended.
quests.deliverable: A link to the published notes: decisions, owners and open questions.
tips: Record decisions and their reasons. The play by play can stay in the room.
Put a name next to every action. Unowned actions dissolve.
quests.duration: One meeting, and an hour to write it up

quests.title: Lead a work day on a shared space
quests.subtitle: Many hands, one morning, a difference you can see.
quests.description: Pick one shared space that needs care, agree the job with whoever looks after it, gather a crew and lead a morning of work. Clearing, building, mending and tidying all count.
quests.impact: A shared space stays usable, and a crew learns to work together.
quests.story: Shared spaces drift until someone gathers a crew. A good work day has one clear job, enough tools and a snack break, and it ends with something everyone can see and use the same afternoon.
quests.firstStep: Walk the space and photograph the one job that would make the biggest difference.
steps: Agree the job, the date and the limits with whoever looks after the space.
Gather tools and materials, and check what is safe to do.
Invite a crew and give each person a clear task.
Work the morning, and stop while people still have energy.
Photograph the result and note anything left for next time.
quests.deliverable: Before and after photos, and a note on what is left to do.
tips: One clear job beats five half finished ones.
Bring water and food. People remember how a work day felt.

quests.title: Start or tend a shared garden bed
quests.subtitle: Learn the ground by feeding it.
quests.description: Take on one garden bed for a season: prepare the soil, plant, water, weed and harvest, and share what grows. If the village has no garden yet, this is how one starts.
quests.impact: Food grown together feeds people and teaches everyone who helps.
quests.story: A single bed is small enough to care for well and big enough to teach a season of lessons. Whatever grows in it ends up on a shared table.
quests.firstStep: Find a spot that gets at least six hours of sun and ask who decides how it is used.
steps: Agree the spot and what to grow with whoever looks after the ground.
Prepare the soil and plant.
Water and weed on a rhythm you can keep, and ask for cover when you are away.
Harvest and share what grows.
Write down what worked so the next season starts ahead.
quests.deliverable: Photos across the season and a note on what grew and what you would change.
tips: Plant less than you think. A small bed kept well beats a big one left to the weeds.
Water in the morning and less is lost to the sun.
quests.duration: A season, an hour or two a week

quests.title: Teach a skill you know
quests.subtitle: Pass on something your hands or head already know.
quests.description: Run a short session teaching something you know well, from bread to bookkeeping. Plan it, invite people, teach it, and leave them with a page of notes.
quests.impact: Every skill shared is one more person in the village who can do it.
quests.story: Every village is full of skills nobody knows about. A short session turns one person's know-how into something several people can do, and it is the easiest way to meet the people who share your interests.
quests.firstStep: Write down three things you could teach in an hour, then pick the one people ask you about most.
steps: Choose the skill and decide what someone will be able to do by the end.
Pick a time and place, and post the invitation.
Gather materials so everyone gets hands on.
Teach it, leave time for questions, and hand out a page of notes.
quests.deliverable: Your notes or handout, and a line on who came.
tips: Teach one thing well. A second session is always possible.
Let people try it while you are still in the room.

quests.title: Photograph a day in the village
quests.subtitle: Show what an ordinary day here looks like.
quests.description: Spend a day or an event photographing what actually happens, then edit a small set and give each picture a sentence of context. Ask before photographing anyone up close.
quests.impact: Honest pictures help the right people find the village, and help the village remember itself.
quests.story: The people meant to find a village usually find it through honest pictures of real days: work in progress, full tables, muddy boots. The same pictures are a gift to the village later, when it wants to remember what this year looked like.
quests.firstStep: Spend twenty minutes photographing one everyday scene, then pick the single frame that tells it best.
steps: Choose a day, an event or a week of small moments.
Photograph what actually happens. Real days make the best pictures.
Ask before photographing people up close, every time.
Edit a small set. Five strong pictures beat fifty loose ones.
Caption each with a sentence of context and share them where the village keeps its pictures.
quests.deliverable: A small edited set with captions, shared where the village can find it.
tips: Early and late light flatter everything.
Whoever looks at these next year needs the caption more than you think.

quests.title: Offer a wellness session
quests.subtitle: Share a practice you are trained in.
quests.description: Offer a session in a practice you are trained in, such as yoga, meditation, massage or movement. Agree the space, set clear agreements at the start, and gather a word of feedback after.
quests.impact: People who are well keep everything else going.
quests.story: A village that works hard needs places to rest and recover. Sessions from trained hands keep people well, and a regular one gives the week a rhythm.
quests.firstStep: Write three sentences about the session: what it is, who it is for, and what to bring.
steps: Confirm the offering and any space or equipment it needs.
Schedule the session and post it where people look for gatherings.
Open with clear consent and comfort agreements.
Gather a word of feedback after, and decide whether it should recur.
quests.deliverable: A note on the session: who came, how it went, and whether it should recur.
tips: Small and regular works better than big and once.
Clear agreements at the start make deeper work possible.

quests.title: Find a rough edge on the village site
quests.subtitle: Make the village's own site easier to use.
quests.description: Use the village's site the way a newcomer would, find the first thing that confuses or breaks, and report it with the steps to see it again. Fix it too, if you can.
quests.impact: Every rough edge smoothed is one less reason for a newcomer to give up.
quests.story: A village's site is shared infrastructure, the same as a path or a kitchen: invisible when it works, and everyone's problem when it does not. A clear report is half of every fix.
quests.firstStep: Spend ten minutes on the site as a newcomer would, and write down the first thing that slowed you down.
steps: Use the site as someone who has never been here.
Write down each rough edge with the steps to see it again.
Add a screenshot for anything you can see.
Pass the report to whoever looks after the site, or fix it yourself if you can.
quests.deliverable: Your report, with steps and screenshots, or a link to what you fixed.
tips: A problem you can make happen twice is half solved.
One clear report beats ten vague ones.

quests.title: Start a music or song circle
quests.subtitle: A few instruments and someone willing to begin.
quests.description: Gather people for an evening of music or singing. A few shared instruments, a song or two everyone knows, and someone to open and close the circle are all it takes.
quests.impact: Singing and playing together is one of the quickest ways a group of people becomes a village.
quests.story: Music is how a village celebrates, grieves and remembers itself. A circle needs no stage and no skill floor, only a few instruments and someone willing to hold it.
quests.firstStep: Pick a date and invite three people directly. A circle of four is already a circle.
steps: Set the time and place, and post the invitation.
Bring or borrow a few shared instruments so nobody needs to own one.
Open simply, with a rhythm or a song anyone can join.
Close while the energy is still warm.
quests.deliverable: A note or a short clip from the circle: who gathered and what was played or sung.
tips: Percussion is the doorway for shy joiners.
Ending on time is what brings people back.

quests.title: Repair something everyone uses
quests.subtitle: Fix the thing everyone has learned to work around.
quests.description: Find something shared that is broken or wearing out, such as a door, a tool, a bench or a tap. Agree the repair with whoever looks after it, and fix it properly.
quests.impact: Shared things that work get used and looked after.
quests.story: Every place has a list of small broken things everyone has learned to step around. Fixing one is honest work with a result you can use the same day, and it shows that shared things here get looked after.
quests.firstStep: Ask three people which shared thing they most often work around, and pick the most common answer.
steps: Agree the repair with whoever looks after the thing.
Gather tools and materials, and check what is safe to do yourself.
Make the repair, and test it.
Note what you used and anything that will need attention again.
quests.deliverable: Before and after photos, and a note on the materials used.
tips: Ask about load and safety before improvising a fix.
Whoever leaves the tools tidy is everyone's favourite builder.

quests._memberTrigger: A founder keeps the ones that fit as real quests and clears the rest.

threads.title: Where should the second water tank go?
threads.body:
We agreed last season that one tank is a single point of failure. The question is siting.

The ridge gives us gravity feed to everything below it, but it is a long pipe run and the delivery truck cannot get up there, so every load would be hand-carried.

Behind the workshop is easy to reach and easy to plumb, but it sits below the main house, so anything uphill needs pumping.

I lean ridge, and I would rather pay the pipe cost once than the pumping cost forever. Curious whether @tomas-example thinks the truck access kills it.

replies.body:
Truck access does not kill it. It changes the cost. Hand-carrying a full load is roughly four person-hours each time, and we would do that maybe twice a year.

Against that, pumping is a pump that fails eventually, plus the power to run it. I think the ridge still wins, but let us cost the pipe run properly before anyone commits.
I priced something similar two years ago. Budget more than you think for the fittings. The pipe itself was the cheap part.

threads.title: Proposal: quiet hours from 9pm to 7am
threads.body:
Raised at three consecutive circle meetings, so it is time to decide it.

**The proposal:** amplified sound and power tools stop at 9pm and do not resume before 7am, across the whole site. Acoustic music, conversation and cooking are unaffected.

**Why:** the workshop and the sleeping cabins are ninety metres apart, and a late job on the bandsaw is audible in every one of them.

**What it costs:** the people who work evenings lose their evenings. That is a real cost and it falls on a specific few, which is exactly why this should be decided openly, by the whole circle.

meta.outcome: Adopted, with a standing exception for harvest week. Revisit after two seasons.

replies.body: Supportive, as long as the harvest-week exception is written in. Every year we forget and every year someone is annoyed.

threads.title: Seed swap and shared lunch, first Sunday
threads.body:
Bring whatever you saved from last season, labelled if you can manage it and honestly guessed if you cannot.

Lunch is shared, so bring a dish as well. There will be more chard than anyone wants; this is the nature of chard.

Newcomers especially welcome: you do not need seeds to come, and taking some home is the entire point.

meta.location: The long table under the big tree

threads.title: The workshop roof goes on Saturday, and we need eight hands
threads.body:
Materials arrive Friday afternoon. We start at seven on Saturday while it is still cool, and we should be done by two.

Bring gloves if you have them. If you have never done this before that is fine, half of us had not either the first time. There will be food.

An announcement is pinned so it stays at the top of the list until it stops mattering. Posting one needs a role that carries it, which is how a village keeps the top of its forum for things that concern everyone.

feed._trigger: A real micropost is published to the feed category
feed._note: Feed items are forum_threads with kind='post' and title NULL in the feed category. heart_count stays 0: a heart is a real ledger send, so hearting an example is refused.

posts.body: Third morning in a row with frost on the low beds. The tomatoes are finished, but the kale has never looked better. Pulling the tomato frames today if anyone wants the stakes.

The pump is fixed. It was the foot valve, not the motor, which is the good outcome: forty minutes and a two-dollar part instead of a new pump.

Water is back on across the whole lower site.
Reminder that the road will be graded on Thursday and the lower gate will be shut from about 8am. Park above the workshop if you need to leave before noon.

tools._note: icon MUST be one of the ten names ToolsHub.tsx allowlists, or it silently renders a wrench.

tools.name: Village Chat
tools.purpose: Day-to-day conversation, quick questions, and anything that does not need to be found again later.
tools.description: The everyday channel. Use it for things that are true today and irrelevant next month. Anything worth finding again belongs in the Forum instead. Chat scrolls away and nobody reads back.
tools.gettingStarted: Ask any member for an invite link, then set your display name to the same handle you use here so people can find you.

tools.name: Shared Documents
tools.purpose: Agreements, meeting notes, budgets and anything the village needs to be able to point at later.
tools.description: The filing cabinet. Meeting notes go in dated folders; agreements live at the top level and are never edited in place. A superseded agreement gets a new file and a note saying what it replaced.
tools.gettingStarted: Read the folder called 'Start here' before adding anything. Naming conventions matter more than they look like they do.

tools.name: Village Calendar
tools.purpose: Work days, gatherings, visitor arrivals and anything that needs more than one person in one place.
tools.description: One shared calendar for the whole village. If an event is not on here it will not be attended, which sounds harsh and is simply true.
tools.gettingStarted: Subscribe to the feed from your own calendar app. That way you actually see the reminders.

tools._memberTrigger: The first tool a founder adds clears them.

library._note: Items are inserted directly, NOT through recordIntake(): intake mints library credits to the donor. Direct rows raise supply-vs-backing coverage without minting anything, which is safe. Borrowing an example is refused; no loan row ever exists.The canner is seeded checked_out so the shelf shows what mid-use looks like:,a grey out-on-loan pill and no Borrow button. NO library_loans row is written.,library_loans has no is_example column, libraryOpenState counts every row with,settled_at IS NULL regardless of escrow, and a loan row would therefore block,turning the module off - the exact trap rule 1 exists to prevent. The item card,renders the borrowed state from library_items.status alone, so a loan row would,buy no pixels and cost the founder their off switch.

items.name: Cordless drill, 18V, two batteries
items.description: The workhorse. Two batteries means one charges while the other works, so please return both. A drill with one battery is half a drill. Comes with the full bit set in the blue case; count the bits back in.

items.name: Broadfork
items.description: Opens compacted beds without inverting the soil layers, which is the whole point of owning one. Heavy enough that it does the work for you if you let it. Do not try to prise rocks with it. The tines will bend.

items.name: Pressure canner, 23 quart
items.description: For low-acid preserving: beans, stock, anything that a water bath will not make safe. The gauge was last tested this year and the rubber gasket is new. Read the manual in the lid before your first run; this is the one library item that can genuinely hurt you.

library._memberTrigger: The first donation the shelf accepts clears them.

stays._note: Rooms and posted prices are pure catalog: no ledger, no Stripe. Booking an example is refused, so no stays row and no open state is ever created. A token price is `amount`, in WHOLE credits as a founder types it, and the seeder converts it once at insert with the token's live decimals (priceToStored). A usd price is `amountMinor`, in cents.

accommodations.name: The Ridge Cabin
accommodations.description: One room with a wood stove, a double bed and a view down the whole valley. Compost toilet and an outdoor shower fed by the tank above it. Warm by mid-morning, bracing before that. The walk up is ten minutes and steeper than it looks.

accommodations.name: Workshop Bunkroom
accommodations.description: Six bunks in the loft above the workshop, shared bathroom below. Where work-exchange visitors and volunteer crews usually land. Cheerfully noisy; the woodshop starts at seven and you will know about it.

accommodations.name: Garden Casita
accommodations.description: A small self-contained house at the edge of the kitchen garden: kitchenette, private bathroom, and a porch that catches the morning. The room longer-stay residents and visiting families ask for, so it books out furthest ahead.

stays._memberTrigger: The first room a founder lists clears them.

commerce._note: payment_products rows are pure catalog for all six kinds, including token_pack. Checkout against an example is refused before any Stripe call.

products.name: Residency application review
products.description: Covers the reading, the two conversations and the reference calls that go into considering a residency application properly. Charged once, whatever the outcome: it pays for the attention, not for a yes.

products.name: Support the land fund
products.description: Goes to the things that outlast any of us: water infrastructure, reforestation, and paying down the land itself. Give what makes sense to you. Every amount is read by a person and acknowledged by one.

products.name: Supporting membership
products.description: A monthly contribution from people who are part of this from a distance. Includes the members-only briefing each lunation and an open invitation to the seasonal gatherings. Cancel any time; nothing is locked in.

_note: Badges carry REAL capability keys and awards held by example identities,
so the page demonstrates the whole arc: definition, grant, holder, stack.
Safe because an example award may only ever point at an example user: the
award route, the claim route and the earned engine all refuse or skip
examples, and example identities never authenticate, so these rows never
reach the capability gate for anyone real. Warning badges never get
awards: a warning award is open state and would block module-off.
Every capability key must exist in shared/capabilities.ts ALL_CAPABILITIES.
One award carries expiresInDays: trust lent for a year, shown on the card as
a date and released by the same clock every read already honours. Never on a
WARNING badge: an unexpired warning award is open state and blocks module-off.
That expiry is a YEAR, and the length is a decision. It is minted forward from
seed time, and every read drops a lapsed award, so a season's worth silently
emptied the holders demo 54 days after a founder enabled badges, on an instance
whose whole point is that it has no real content yet. Nothing renews it: the
refresh one-shots are permanent per id. A year outlives realistic retirement,
so the card teaches lapsing trust without going blank on anyone.

badges.name: First Harvest
badges.description: Brought in the first crop of the season. Granted by a steward who witnessed the work.

awards.note: Three baskets of squash from the north beds.

badges.name: Village Steward
badges.description: Carries the village's trust to moderate the forum, post announcements and record the land's measurements. Powers travel with the badge and leave with it, and this one is lent for a year.

awards.note: Stewarding through the wet season. The village lends this for one year at a time.

badges.name: Ten Times Useful
badges.description: Ten quests consented by others. The engine awards this on its own at cycle close, and it stacks: twenty quests earns it twice. It carries no powers, which is what most earned badges are for.

awards.note: Earned twice over: twenty-three consented quests.

badges.name: Gardener
badges.description: A self-claimed identity: tell the village what you do with your hands. Self badges grant nothing; they help people find each other.

badges.name: Posting Paused
badges.description: A deliberate brake: while this is held, forum posting is closed to the holder. A deny beats every role and stage; only an admin outranks it.

badges._memberTrigger: The first badge this village defines clears them.

health._note: Snapshots need >= 3 distinct cycle_number values before trends unlock, so examples span three lunations. Metric keys come from the closed set in shared/healthMetrics.ts. A new key cannot be invented here.

regenEntries.note: Mixed natives along the north boundary and through the erosion gully, mostly nitrogen fixers to hold the bank, with fruit interplanted where there is enough light. Counted at planting, not at survival; the honest survival number comes next dry season.
Capacity of the new catchment plus the swale system on the north slope. This is water that used to leave the property within a day of falling.
The overgrazed section below the ridge, now fenced off from stock and replanted. Absolute area under active restoration, not a claim that it is finished.

health._memberTrigger: The first measurement a steward records clears them.

resources._note: Declarations only, never balances. Scope ids point at the map's example circles and progression's example seats, so the lens draws whole while those stand. Amounts are minor units; CHF is the platform default currency (P8).

spendingRules.note: Seeds, small tools, fuel for the pump: the everyday things the land asks for.
Bigger purchases for the land pass through the circle before the treasury pays.
The steward keeps the work moving without asking for every bag of lime.
Anything that changes the land itself waits for the founders' yes.

fundingSources.name: Guest stays
fundingSources.note: Nights hosted on the land carry the largest share of the year.

fundingSources.name: A restoration grant
fundingSources.note: A three year grant for watershed repair, drawn down as the work lands.

circleBudgets.note: The land circle's standing envelope for a season of ordinary work.

recordings.title: Weekly circle call: water siting and the winter build

segments.text: Alright, we are recording. Two things today: where the second tank goes, and whether the winter build is still realistic given where we are on materials.

On the tank: I walked the ridge line again on Sunday. Gravity feed reaches everything below it, including the bunkroom, which the workshop site does not. The catch is the truck cannot get up there, so every delivery is hand-carried.

I can cost the pipe run properly by Friday if that would settle it. My instinct is that the pipe is cheaper than a pump plus the power to run it over ten years, but I would rather show numbers than instincts.
Please do. And on the winter build: we are short on the roofing steel and the supplier has gone quiet. Somebody needs to chase that this week or we lose the dry window entirely.
I will chase the supplier. If they cannot commit to a date by Wednesday we should price a second source and stop waiting politely.

synthesis.aiBody:
The call covered two decisions.

**Water tank siting.** The ridge site gives gravity feed to the entire lower site including the bunkroom; the workshop site does not. The objection is delivery access: the ridge cannot take a truck, so every load is hand-carried. A full pipe-run costing was offered to settle it by Friday, on the reasoning that pipe is a one-time cost while pumping is perpetual.

**Winter build.** Roofing steel is short and the supplier has stopped responding. The dry window is at risk. Agreement that the supplier is chased this week, with a second source priced if no firm date arrives by Wednesday.
synthesis.body:

**Winter build**: the roofing steel is the bottleneck and the supplier has gone quiet. Being chased this week. If there's no firm date by Wednesday we stop waiting politely and price a second source.

(This is the human-edited copy. The untouched AI version sits beside it, and that pairing is the point: nothing publishes itself.)

Second roofing-steel supplier to be priced if the current one gives no firm date by Wednesday.

sharedItems.title: Looking for a timber framer for a two-week build
sharedItems.detail:
We are raising a 6x8 metre workshop frame next season and have the timber milled and stacked, but nobody here has cut joinery at this scale before.

We can offer accommodation, all meals, and stay credits for the duration. What we are really after is someone willing to teach while they work. We want to come out of it with four people who can do it again.

sharedItems.title: Surplus fruit tree seedlings, free to a good home
sharedItems.detail:
Roughly ninety seedlings surplus to our own planting: citrus, avocado, and a lot of guava. Twelve to eighteen months old, bare-rooted and ready to travel.

Free to any village on the network. We would ask you to collect, and to tell us in a year how many made it. We are trying to learn which rootstock actually survives transplant.

sharedItems.title: Our water catchment design, drawings and costings included
sharedItems.detail:
We spent two years and more money than we needed to getting our catchment right. The drawings, the parts list and the honest account of what we would do differently are yours for the asking.

Particularly relevant if you are on a slope with a long dry season. Happy to walk someone through it on a call.

items.title: Two experienced natural builders available in the off season
items.detail: Cob and lime plaster mostly, some light timber work. Available for roughly six weeks after our harvest finishes. They would want accommodation and food; beyond that they are looking for interesting work, not income.

items.title: Seeking a shared bulk order for organic seed
items.detail: Our supplier's minimum is well above what one village uses in a season, and the per-unit price at volume is roughly half. Looking for two or three villages to split an order and the freight.

_note: Example TOKENS (registry rows, is_example=1) plus listings and posted prices,
all display-only. exampleStock is a presentation number on the settings row;
the ledger holds NO rows for example tokens, so conservation holds trivially
and the buy route refuses the example before any stock logic runs.
Only credit-kind tokens can list (recognition and Hypha-governed refuse, and
the boot firewalls re-prove that every deploy). The village creating or
listing its own token retires the whole set, registry rows included.

prices.note: One credit to one dollar, chosen for legibility: everyone can price a favour, a meal or an hour without arithmetic. Revisit once the village has its own sense of value.
Covers materials and the teacher's time for one session. Priced to break even, never to profit from learning.

_note: `entries` STAYS EMPTY, permanently. A gratitude row posts to the ledger at
creation (sendGratitude -> postTransfer from the recognition faucet), so an
example send would either mint real recognition to a real member or break the
per-token conservation invariant that refuses boot.
`voices` is how the wall gets something true to open with anyway. A voice has
no sender, no recipient and no amount, so it is not a send: it never reaches
the ledger and conservation holds trivially. The table it seeds into
(gratitude_voices, migration 0180) has nowhere to record who gave what to
whom. That absence is the safety property, and it is deliberate.
WHAT THESE SIXTEEN ARE FOR, which is more than filling a blank page. A founder
opening a new village reads them before they write anything, and every thanks
written afterwards is shaped by the register they set. So they are second
person, addressed to one person, about one thing that happened, and they span
the kinds of care a village runs on including the ones people forget to name.
Write them vaguely and the village learns vagueness.
Platform-generic, so no village, place, role or token is named and every fork
inherits the same sixteen. scripts/check-voice.mjs reads these string values
like any other shipped copy.

voices.message: You carried water to the new beds every morning for a week and never mentioned it once.
You took the compost shift in the rain, twice, and did not put your name down either time.
You spent three Saturdays pulling plastic out of the riverbed, and the fish came back.
You organised the fire ceremony from the first log to the last song.
You mapped every water line on the land so the next person will not have to guess.
You ran the seed swap, and people came who had never come to anything.
You rebuilt the washhouse roof before the rains, with whoever turned up.
You sat with me on the steps when I could not talk about it yet.
You asked me a second time, after I said I was fine the first time.
You showed me how to sharpen the blade properly, and then let me ruin two before I got it.
You cooked for eleven people on the night the power went out.
You kept a plate warm for me because you knew what time I finish.
You noticed the gate was hanging wrong and fixed it before anyone filed a complaint.
You saw that I had gone quiet and you came and found me at the end.
You made space in the meeting for the person who had not spoken yet.
You stayed to stack the chairs when everyone else had gone home.
